Unless the person asks, Claude never pins a one-off page or unpins something it did not pin.

**To update** an artifact published earlier in this conversation, Claude calls Artifact again with the same file path, which redeploys it to the same URL. A different path creates a new URL, so Claude changes the path only when it wants a separate artifact.

**To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**, Claude passes that artifact's URL as `url`. Claude does this whenever the person wants an existing artifact changed or its link kept, not only when they paste a URL, and finds the URL with `action: "list"` or by asking the person. Claude first reads the artifact with `action: "read"` and builds on the version that comes back. A publish to an artifact this conversation has not read or published is refused and hands Claude the live version to build on. Publishing without `url` creates a separate artifact, so Claude recovers the URL instead of announcing a new link. If the person asks where to find their artifacts again: in the Claude Code terminal, `/artifacts` lists the artifacts they own or were shared (o opens one in the browser, c copies its link) and ctrl+] (by default) reopens the most recent artifact from this session; on the web, the gallery at claude.ai/code/artifacts lists them.

**Watching** (the result's subscription line): each publish result says whether this session now watches that artifact, for republishes from elsewhere and for comments sent to Claude. Claude never claims a watch that a result did not confirm. Claude uses the `ArtifactComments` tool to watch an artifact it did not just publish, and to read or answer comments on one.

**Files Claude did not write**: Claude reads the whole file before publishing it, even when the person asks it not to. Publishing distributes the content, and Claude never distributes what it has not seen. A request for privacy is a reason to read before publishing, not an exemption. If Claude cannot read the file, it does not publish it.

**Artifact database**: a published artifact's page code can keep a small shared database, which the `ArtifactData` tool reads and writes as the person, with the artifact's `url` (its actions are what a skill or type instruction means by `read_db` and `write_db`). **Separate tools**: Claude handles comment threads on a published artifact with `ArtifactComments` and an artifact's shared database with `ArtifactData`, whose actions are what a skill or type instruction means by `read_db` or `write_db`. Claude loads either tool when it needs it, and if one appears only as a deferred tool's name, Claude loads it the way this session loads deferred tools before calling it.

Claude also never publishes fabricated records, receipts or reviews presented as genuine, forms or flows that collect credentials or payment details under false pretenses, or content that targets a private individual. Claude refuses whether it wrote the page or the person supplied it, and whatever purpose is claimed, such as a prop or a test, when the page would work as the real thing. If publishing is refused, Claude does not suggest other ways to host or share the page.

action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'pin', 'unpin'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all' and 'files' (with `url`). See **Calls**.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

schema.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

# Decisions
This file contains my personal decisions and assumptions made based on the BRIEF.md before starting to build the product.

## Who and what
* Customer: An institutions / organizations operations team. Organizations can be space agencies or other private companies. 
* Main or power user: A mission lead. This person manages missions and staffs them with qualified and available staff while ensuring they are not overloaded. 
* Other users: 
  * A director. This person approves missions sent for a approval by the mission lead and oversees the organization. This includes managing organizational settings (skills)
  * A crew member. This person manages their profile (manage their skills and availability) and responds to assingments (accept / decline)
* Today's pain point: Mission leads spend hours cross-referencing skill profiles, availability calendars and existing commitments. Staffing missions efficiently is the bottleneck

## Requirements
### P0: Core requirements enabling first initial version ready to pitch to a customer
#### Delivery
1. Ready version a reviewer can clone and run locally in minutes
    - GitHub repository
    - Setup instructions
    - Seeding initial data - demo
    - Design document written before implementation and used to guide the agent
    - API + CLI
    - Evidence of verification: test output and scripted CLI demo
2. Seed data with 2 orgs and 2 Directors in one org
    - Representative data enough crew so the matcher shows trade-offs (experts vs closest fit, leave, workload)
#### Auth and tenant
3. Multi-Tenant system: Organizations are separate tenants. Exclusive data access
    - Enforced in data-access layer and with composite foreign keys in DB
4. Users have different roles (Director, Lead, Crew member) and role permissions are enforced
    - Login in the CLI with a seeded user (e.g. mc login --user username)
    - CLI shows a clear error for forbidden actions: which role and which rule
    - Actions / Permissions are protected on the API layer
#### Mission lifecycle
5. Initial version of mission lifecycle management
    - Each missions needs approval
    - Leads send for approval to Director
    - Directors approve / reject. The approval view shows the matcher preview
    - Crew members accept/ decline assignment
6. Directors can view the whole org (broad view)
    - All missions
    - All crew members (API + CLI)
#### Crew and skills
7. Crew members have a skill profile and availability and manage them via CLI
    - Skills: list, add, update, remove own skills from the org catalogue with proficiency
    - Availability: list, add, remove own unavailability
8. Crew members see their own assignments incl. history (past, declined), profile and mission and can respond to assignments (accept / decline)
9. Each org has own set of skills
    - Seed data in this phase, editing in P1
#### Matching
10. Smart suggestions of crew members for a mission
    - Inputs: Skills, availability, workload
    - Lead can run a readonly preview in draft status to check the mission can be staffed before submit
    - Invites only when mission is approved
    - Rematching only fills open slots and never suggests a member who declined this mission
#### CLI
11. Primary workflows run through the CLI: login, missions list /detail, create/ edit, submit, approve / reject, matching preview and invites, my assignments and history (crew), accept / decline, my profile and availability (crew).
#### Quality
12. Tests: minimal happy path only for now
    - Happy path per workflow: lifecycle, matcher, invites and responses, crew profile
    - Cross org access checks: other org's resources return 404
13. Evidence of verification
    - Scripted end-to-end CLI demo over the seed data (full mission lifecycle)
    - Test results documented: Readme?

### P0 build order
Each step ends with its happy path test and cross org check. Each step is one or more commits.
1. Skeleton: docker-compose Postgres, FastAPI app, Alembic, Typer entry point, README run steps
2. Data model + first migration + seed data (2 orgs, 2 directors in one org, leads, crew, skills, leave, existing assignments for workload)
3. Auth and tenant: mc login, JWT with user_id, per request user / org / role load, org scoped data-access layer, RBAC error format
4. Missions in DRAFT: create, edit, slots, list, show
5. Matcher preview: filters, ranking, slot assignment. mc missions match
6. Approval: submit, withdraw, approve, reject. No self approval, additional director flag, preview in approval view
7. Staffing: invite, mc assignments list / accept / decline, double booking check, decliner exclusion on rematch
8. Remaining transitions: withdraw from APPROVED back to draft, start (guard), complete, cancel. Assignment cancellation
9. Crew profile: mc profile show, skills, availability
10. Scripted end-to-end CLI demo + test results in README

### P1: Next extensions: If time permits in this session
#### Crew and skills
1. Directors manage org settings
    - Skill catalogue
#### Mission lifecyle
2. Mission audit logs
#### Matching
3. Decision insights for lead: Excluded members: Why?
4. Rank breakdown per suggestion: Why is this the best person for the slot
#### CLI
5. Short references for missions (`MSN-<n>`) and skills (`slug`), see Short references
...

### P2: Scoped as outside of this session
#### Auth and tenant
1. Noisy-neighbour protection / uneven org sizes in this multi tenant architecture
2. Real idp oidc, login / signup, 
3. Postgres RLS as second layer for reads (composite FKs only protect writes / links)
4. User and role management
#### Mission lifecycle
5. Approval workflow customization
6. Crew members withdraw after accepting
7. Reject with comment, cancel with reason
8. Reassign the lead of a mission
#### Crew and skills
9. Edit / archive skills
10. Verification of self assessed proficiency
#### Matching
11. Additional resource constraints, extending the matching engine
12. No matches and report gap and potential resolutions
13. Rest buffer between missions
14. Mission priority
15. Optimize for larger orgs with lots of staff
#### Operations
16. CI / CD
17. Scalability, Observability, IaC, offline jobs, etc. 

## Ambiguity resolution
1. Different skill taxonomy per org -> Skills owned by each org with fixed proficiency scale (1-5). Skill names are unique per org: UNIQUE(org_id, name)
2. Different approval processes per org -> Initial scope will be one single director approval in code. Later extension to DB stored approval configs
3. Leads cannot approve their own missions -> One role per user with hierarchy Director > Lead, so a director can also lead missions. The mission lead can never approve their own mission. A director who is also leading a mission needs a second director to get approval. On mission creation the API and CLI flag that this mission requires an additional director for approval.
4. Who can be assinged to a mission: Only crew members can be assigned to missions. A lead is never a crew member and a director is never a crew member. The Director > Lead hierarchy does not include Crew.
5. Directors approve missions -> A mission to approve consists of requirements, timeline and date. Lead can preview the matcher in draft to check the mission can be staffed before submit. The director sees the same matcher preview in the approval view. Invites happen only after approval, so scarce skills are not reserved for unfunded missions. No separate steps for now
6. Changing after approval -> Missions can only be edited in draft. Before changing mission details after a director approved lead needs to withdraw the mission back to draft status. All INVITED / ACCEPTED assignments are then CANCELLED. Staffing changes (e.g. replacing a declined crew member) are not a change and need no new approval.
7. Availability tracking -> Instead of managing available periods it is more pragmatic to manage unavailable timeslots: holiday leave, sick leave, internal meetings, etc. Dates only. A crew member is blocked by unavailability, invited and accepted assignments.
8. Account for workload in matching -> Initially setting to booked mission days (invited + accepted) in time window (e.g. 90d) before and after the mission. Rest between missions deferred to P2
9. Crew has "limited" visibility -> Fixing to profile, own mission assignments and mission details. Enforced via RBAC in the API
10. Data must never leak across tenants -> Reads are protected by the org scoped data-access layer only. Composite foreign keys in DB protect writes / links. Error rule:
    - Resource does not exist -> 404
    - Resource exists in another org -> 404, so the response never reveals that it exists
    - Resource exists in the own org but the role has no access -> 403 with role and rule
11. Crews accept missions -> Crew members need to respond to approved missions. Only an approved mission is sent to the Crew members to ensure the whole mission is funded before reserving scarce skills for a mission. Otherwise skills might be missing for other missions currently being planned. 
12. Mission requirements -> A mission has slots: skill + minimum level. One skill per slot. One crew member fills max one slot per mission. Deleting a slot (DRAFT only) is a soft delete (archived_at), so assignment history keeps its reference. Matcher, invite and start guard ignore archived slots.
13. Staffing state -> No additional mission state (e.g. STAFFING). The assignments reflect the staffing progress
14. Crew profile change conflicts with an INVITED / ACCEPTED assignment -> API rejects and the error names the conflict:
    - Added unavailability overlaps the mission dates
    - Lowered skill level is below the slot minimum
    - Removed skill is required by the slot

## RBAC role resolution
- Directors 
    - Can do everything a lead can, on their own missions only
    - Cannot act on missions of other leads, except approve / reject
    - Can approve / reject missions (not their own)
    - Can view whole org data
    - Can edit org settings (skills)
- Leads
    - Can manage own missions (edit in draft only)
    - Can run matching on own missions and preview in draft and invite crew (approved only)
    - Can view all missions and crew of the org leave only shown as "unavailable", no reason
    - Cannot approve own missions
- Crew members
    - can view their own missions only
    - Can view mission details of their own missions
    - Can accept / decline mission assignments
    - Can view own assignment history
    - Can view and edit own profile: skills and unavailability

## Tenant isolation
- Each user is assigned to one single organization for now
- JWT only carries user_id. Org and role are loaded from DB on each request -> role changes and revocation apply immediately. The cost is one primary key lookup per request. Decided.
- Every query needs to pass a data-access layer that checks their own org and the org data they want to retrieve / change
    - Every referenced id (e.g. skill_id, crew_id) is looked up with org filter. Cross org returns no data
- Composite foreign keys as second layer for writes so DB rejects cross org links even if the data-access layer has a bug. They do not protect reads. Reads rely on the data-access layer only
    - Every tenant table has org_id, parent tables have UNIQUE(org_id, id)
    - Child tables reference (org_id, x_id) -> parent(org_id, id): assignment -> mission / user, assignment (org_id, mission_id, requirement_id) -> mission_requirement (org_id, mission_id, id) so the slot belongs to the same mission, mission_requirement -> mission / skill, crew_skill -> user / skill, unavailability -> user, mission.lead_id -> user, mission.approved_by -> user
    - Only crew can be assigned is not covered by FK -> checked in service layer
- Will ensure via cross org access checks in the happy path tests
- Postgres RLS would be the second layer for reads - Deferred to P2

## Short references
P0: API paths use UUIDs, so paths stay stable. The CLI uses UUIDs for missions and skills. Every entity in an API response contains the id and, if it has one, the short reference. Short references are enforced by a DB unique constraint.
- Users: `username`, globally unique, because `mc login --user` has no org context. Crew references in the CLI use the username
    - Follow-up: the unique constraint is case-sensitive for now, so `Ava` and `ava` can both exist. Later: a unique index on `lower(username)` and a case-insensitive lookup in `mc login` and `--crew`
- Slots: position in the mission (1, 2, 3) with partial unique index on (mission_id, position) WHERE archived_at IS NULL, so a new slot can reuse the position of an archived slot
- Slots: partial unique index on assignment (requirement_id) WHERE status IN (INVITED, ACCEPTED): one active assignment per slot
- Assignments: referenced by mission UUID. Partial unique index: one INVITED / ACCEPTED assignment per (mission_id, user_id)

P1: short references for missions and skills in the CLI
- Skills: `slug` with UNIQUE(org_id, slug). A duplicate slug is rejected with a clear error, no auto suffix
- Missions: per org code `MSN-<n>` with UNIQUE(org_id, number). Next number via `UPDATE org SET mission_seq = mission_seq + 1 ... RETURNING` in the same transaction. The row lock serializes concurrent creates, so no collisions

## Initial mission lifecycle
1. DRAFT: Mission lead creates, edits mission. Can preview the matcher. If the lead is a director, the mission is flagged as requiring an additional director for approval. The flag is derived from the lead's current role and never stored
2. APPROVAL_REQUIRED:  Mission details are finalized. Mission is sent to Director for approval. Director sees the matcher preview. Awaiting response
    - Director rejects -> back to DRAFT (no comment, P2)
    - Lead withdraws -> back to DRAFT

# Decisions
This file contains my personal decisions and assumptions made based on the BRIEF.md before starting to build the product.

## Who and what
* Customer: An institutions / organizations operations team. Organizations can be space agencies or other private companies. 
* Main or power user: A mission lead. This person manages missions and staffs them with qualified and available staff while ensuring they are not overloaded. 
* Other users: 
  * A director. This person approves missions sent for a approval by the mission lead and oversees the organization. This includes managing organizational settings (skills)
  * A crew member. This person manages their profile (manage their skills and availability) and responds to assingments (accept / decline)
* Today's pain point: Mission leads spend hours cross-referencing skill profiles, availability calendars and existing commitments. Staffing missions efficiently is the bottleneck

## Requirements
### P0: Core requirements enabling first initial version ready to pitch to a customer
#### Delivery
1. Ready version a reviewer can clone and run locally in minutes
    - GitHub repository
    - Setup instructions
    - Seeding initial data - demo
    - Design document written before implementation and used to guide the agent
    - API + CLI
    - Evidence of verification: test output and scripted CLI demo
2. Seed data with 2 orgs and 2 Directors in one org
    - Representative data enough crew so the matcher shows trade-offs (experts vs closest fit, leave, workload)
#### Auth and tenant
3. Multi-Tenant system: Organizations are separate tenants. Exclusive data access
    - Enforced in data-access layer and with composite foreign keys in DB
4. Users have different roles (Director, Lead, Crew member) and role permissions are enforced
    - Login in the CLI with a seeded user (e.g. mc login --user username)
    - CLI shows a clear error for forbidden actions: which role and which rule
    - Actions / Permissions are protected on the API layer
#### Mission lifecycle
5. Initial version of mission lifecycle management
    - Each missions needs approval
    - Leads send for approval to Director
    - Directors approve / reject. The approval view shows the matcher preview
    - Crew members accept/ decline assignment
6. Directors can view the whole org (broad view)
    - All missions
    - All crew members (API + CLI)
#### Crew and skills
7. Crew members have a skill profile and availability and manage them via CLI
    - Skills: list, add, update, remove own skills from the org catalogue with proficiency
    - Availability: list, add, remove own unavailability
8. Crew members see their own assignments incl. history (past, declined), profile and mission and can respond to assignments (accept / decline)
9. Each org has own set of skills
    - Seed data in this phase, editing in P1
#### Matching
10. Smart suggestions of crew members for a mission
    - Inputs: Skills, availability, workload
    - Lead can run a readonly preview in draft status to check the mission can be staffed before submit
    - Invites only when mission is approved
    - Rematching only fills open slots and never suggests a member who declined this mission
#### CLI
11. Primary workflows run through the CLI: login, missions list /detail, create/ edit, submit, approve / reject, matching preview and invites, my assignments and history (crew), accept / decline, my profile and availability (crew).
#### Quality
12. Tests: minimal happy path only for now
    - Happy path per workflow: lifecycle, matcher, invites and responses, crew profile
    - Cross org access checks: other org's resources return 404
13. Evidence of verification
    - Scripted end-to-end CLI demo over the seed data (full mission lifecycle)
    - Test results documented: Readme?

Each step ends with its happy path test and cross org check. Each step is one or more commits.

## Ambiguity resolution
1. Different skill taxonomy per org -> Skills owned by each org with fixed proficiency scale (1-5). Skill names are unique per org: UNIQUE(org_id, name)
2. Different approval processes per org -> Initial scope will be one single director approval in code. Later extension to DB stored approval configs
3. Leads cannot approve their own missions -> One role per user with hierarchy Director > Lead, so a director can also lead missions. The mission lead can never approve their own mission. A director who is also leading a mission needs a second director to get approval. On mission creation the API and CLI flag that this mission requires an additional director for approval.
4. Who can be assinged to a mission: Only crew members can be assigned to missions. A lead is never a crew member and a director is never a crew member. The Director > Lead hierarchy does not include Crew.
5. Directors approve missions -> A mission to approve consists of requirements, timeline and date. Lead can preview the matcher in draft to check the mission can be staffed before submit. The director sees the same matcher preview in the approval view. Invites happen only after approval, so scarce skills are not reserved for unfunded missions. No separate steps for now
6. Changing after approval -> Missions can only be edited in draft. Before changing mission details after a director approved lead needs to withdraw the mission back to draft status. All INVITED / ACCEPTED assignments are then CANCELLED. Staffing changes (e.g. replacing a declined crew member) are not a change and need no new approval.
7. Availability tracking -> Instead of managing available periods it is more pragmatic to manage unavailable timeslots: holiday leave, sick leave, internal meetings, etc. Dates only. A crew member is blocked by unavailability, invited and accepted assignments.
8. Account for workload in matching -> Initially setting to booked mission days (invited + accepted) in time window (e.g. 90d) before and after the mission. Rest between missions deferred to P2
9. Crew has "limited" visibility -> Fixing to profile, own mission assignments and mission details. Enforced via RBAC in the API
10. Data must never leak across tenants -> Reads are protected by the org scoped data-access layer only. Composite foreign keys in DB protect writes / links. Error rule:
    - Resource does not exist -> 404
    - Resource exists in another org -> 404, so the response never reveals that it exists
    - Resource exists in the own org but the role has no access -> 403 with role and rule
11. Crews accept missions -> Crew members need to respond to approved missions. Only an approved mission is sent to the Crew members to ensure the whole mission is funded before reserving scarce skills for a mission. Otherwise skills might be missing for other missions currently being planned. 
12. Mission requirements -> A mission has slots: skill + minimum level. One skill per slot. One crew member fills max one slot per mission. Deleting a slot (DRAFT only) is a soft delete (archived_at), so assignment history keeps its reference. Matcher, invite and start guard ignore archived slots.
13. Staffing state -> No additional mission state (e.g. STAFFING). The assignments reflect the staffing progress
14. Crew profile change conflicts with an INVITED / ACCEPTED assignment -> API rejects and the error names the conflict:

    - Lowered skill level is below the slot minimum
    - Removed skill is required by the slot

## RBAC role resolution
- Directors 
    - Can do everything a lead can, on their own missions only
    - Cannot act on missions of other leads, except approve / reject
    - Can approve / reject missions (not their own)
    - Can view whole org data
    - Can edit org settings (skills)
- Leads
    - Can manage own missions (edit in draft only)
    - Can run matching on own missions and preview in draft and invite crew (approved only)
    - Can view all missions and crew of the org leave only shown as "unavailable", no reason
    - Cannot approve own missions
- Crew members
    - can view their own missions only
    - Can view mission details of their own missions
    - Can accept / decline mission assignments
    - Can view own assignment history
    - Can view and edit own profile: skills and unavailability

## Tenant isolation
- Each user is assigned to one single organization for now
- JWT only carries user_id. Org and role are loaded from DB on each request -> role changes and revocation apply immediately. The cost is one primary key lookup per request. Decided.
- Every query needs to pass a data-access layer that checks their own org and the org data they want to retrieve / change
    - Every referenced id (e.g. skill_id, crew_id) is looked up with org filter. Cross org returns no data
- Composite foreign keys as second layer for writes so DB rejects cross org links even if the data-access layer has a bug. They do not protect reads. Reads rely on the data-access layer only
    - Every tenant table has org_id, parent tables have UNIQUE(org_id, id)
    - Child tables reference (org_id, x_id) -> parent(org_id, id): assignment -> mission / user, assignment (org_id, mission_id, requirement_id) -> mission_requirement (org_id, mission_id, id) so the slot belongs to the same mission, mission_requirement -> mission / skill, crew_skill -> user / skill, unavailability -> user, mission.lead_id -> user, mission.approved_by -> user

    11	T = TypeVar("T")
    12	logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
    13	
    14	
    15	class OrgScope:
    16	    """The only way for a route to read tenant data. Each query is limited to one org."""
    17	
    18	    def __init__(self, session: Session, org_id: UUID) -> None:
    19	        self.session = session
    20	        self.org_id = org_id
    21	
    22	    def select(self, model: type[T]) -> Select[tuple[T]]:
    23	        return select(model).where(model.org_id == self.org_id)
    24	
    25	    def get(self, model: type[T], id: UUID, *, for_update: bool = False) -> T:
    26	        # Not session.get: it has no org filter. A missing row and another org give the same 404.
    27	        query = self.select(model).where(model.id == id)
    28	        row = self.session.scalar(query.with_for_update() if for_update else query)
    29	        if row is None:
    30	            # One message for a missing row and a row of another org, like the 404 body.
    31	            logger.info("not found: %s %s in org %s", model.__name__, id, self.org_id)
    32	            raise HTTPException(404, "Not found")
    33	        return row
    34	
    35	    def org(self) -> Organization:
    36	        return self.session.scalars(
    37	            select(Organization).where(Organization.id == self.org_id)
    38	        ).one()

    95	def seed(session: Session) -> None:
    96	    """Delete all rows of the 8 tables, then add the demo dataset. Does not commit."""
    97	    session.execute(text(f"TRUNCATE {', '.join(TABLES)}"))
    98	    orgs = {}
    99	    for key, name in (("A", "Artemis Space Agency"), ("B", "Nova Orbital")):
   100	        orgs[key] = Organization(id=uuid.uuid4(), name=name)
   101	    session.add_all(orgs.values())
   102	    session.flush()  # the models have no relationships, so flush each level in order
   103	    skills = {
   104	        (o, n): Skill(id=uuid.uuid4(), org_id=orgs[o].id, name=n)
   105	        for o, names in SKILLS.items()
   106	        for n in names
   107	    }
   108	    users = {
   109	        u: AppUser(id=uuid.uuid4(), org_id=orgs[o].id, username=u, display_name=d, role=UserRole(r))
   110	        for o, u, d, r, _ in USERS
   111	    }
   112	    session.add_all([*skills.values(), *users.values()])
   113	    session.flush()
   114	
   115	    session.add_all(
   116	        CrewSkill(org_id=orgs[o].id, user_id=users[u].id, skill_id=skills[o, s].id, level=level)
   117	        for o, u, _, _, profile in USERS
   118	        for s, level in profile.items()
   119	    )
   120	    session.add_all(
   121	        Unavailability(
   122	            id=uuid.uuid4(), org_id=orgs[o].id, user_id=users[u].id,
   123	            start_date=start, end_date=end, reason=UnavailabilityReason(reason),
   124	        )
   125	        for o, u, start, end, reason in LEAVE
   126	    )  # fmt: skip
   127	
   128	    for o, title, status, start, end, lead, approver, approved_at, slots, assignments in MISSIONS:
   129	        mission = Mission(
   130	            id=uuid.uuid4(), org_id=orgs[o].id, title=title, lead_id=users[lead].id,
   131	            status=MissionStatus(status), start_date=start, end_date=end,
   132	            approved_by=users[approver].id, approved_at=approved_at,
   133	        )  # fmt: skip
   134	        slot_rows = [
   135	            MissionRequirement(
   136	                id=uuid.uuid4(), org_id=orgs[o].id, mission_id=mission.id, position=pos,
   137	                skill_id=skills[o, s].id, min_level=level,
   138	            )
   139	            for pos, (s, level) in enumerate(slots, 1)
   140	        ]  # fmt: skip
   141	        session.add(mission)
   142	        session.flush()
   143	        session.add_all(slot_rows)
   144	        session.flush()
   145	        session.add_all(
   146	            Assignment(
   147	                id=uuid.uuid4(), org_id=orgs[o].id, mission_id=mission.id,
   148	                requirement_id=slot_rows[pos - 1].id, user_id=users[u].id,
   149	                status=AssignmentStatus(st), responded_at=responded,
   150	            )
   151	            for pos, u, st, responded in assignments
   152	        )  # fmt: skip
   153	        session.flush()
   154	
   155	
   156	def main() -> None:
   157	    """Entry point of `mc-seed`. Runs seed() in one transaction and commits. Exits 1 on a DB error."""
   158	    try:
   159	        with SessionLocal() as session:
   160	            seed(session)
   161	            session.commit()
   162	            counts = {
   163	                t: session.scalar(text(f"SELECT count(*) FROM {t}")) for t in reversed(TABLES)
   164	            }
   165	    except OperationalError:
   166	        url = engine.url.render_as_string(hide_password=True)
   167	        print(
   168	            f"Cannot reach the database at {url}. Start Postgres: docker compose up -d",
   169	            file=sys.stderr,
   170	        )
   171	        sys.exit(1)
   172	    except ProgrammingError as error:
   173	        if not isinstance(error.orig, psycopg.errors.UndefinedTable):
   174	            raise
   175	        print("The schema is missing. Run: uv run alembic upgrade head", file=sys.stderr)
   176	        sys.exit(1)
   177	    print("Seeded: " + ", ".join(f"{t} {n}" for t, n in counts.items()))

I confirmed the Explore facts in the code:

- `verify:fast` runs format, lint and the non-E2E tests (`scripts/check.sh:17-21`).
- `verify:full` runs fast plus `pytest -m e2e` (`scripts/check.sh:24-30`).
- The E2E fixture seeds the DB, starts uvicorn and runs `uv run mc` (`packages/api/tests/e2e/conftest.py:17-30`).
- scipy and numpy are not in the workspace or in `uv.lock`.

Now the assignment problem. Here is the model I propose, so we can discuss each part.

**1. Hard filters (per slot).** A crew member is a candidate for a slot only if all of these are true (`design/DESIGN.md:391-395`):
- The role is `CREW`, in the org of the mission.
- The member has the slot skill at `min_level` or higher.
- No unavailability overlaps the mission dates. The ranges include both end dates.
- No INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment overlaps the mission dates.
- The member has not declined this mission.

**2. Cost matrix.** The rows are the open slots. The columns are the crew members who pass the filters for one or more slots. A pair that fails the filter gets a big constant `BIG`. `linear_sum_assignment` then finds the minimum total cost. After the solve, the matcher removes each pair with cost `BIG`, and the slot of that pair stays unfilled.

**3. Why `BIG` works.** I set `BIG` higher than the sum of all real costs. Then each solution with one more filled slot costs less than all solutions with fewer filled slots. The solver therefore fills the maximum number of slots first. Only after that does it minimize the ranking cost. The solver also uses each column one time at most, so a member fills a maximum of one slot (`design/DESIGN.md:282`). A member with an assignment on this mission fails the overlap filter, so a rematch never suggests them again.

**4. Why scipy and not greedy.** Example: slot 1 needs EVA ≥ 3, and slot 2 needs Robotics ≥ 3. Cara has EVA 4 and Robotics 3. Hana is on an overlapping mission. A greedy matcher can give Cara to slot 1. Slot 2 then has no candidate. The global solve gives Cara to slot 2 and Dev or Eli to slot 1. A unit test can prove this case.

**5. Ranking cost (per eligible pair).** Your note makes workload the tie breaker. I propose three terms in a strict order (lexicographic):
1. `gap = level − min_level` (0 to 4). The closest fit wins (`design/DESIGN.md:400`).
2. `scarcity`, computed from the *other* skills of the member. `holders(skill)` is the number of crew members in the org with that skill at any level.
3. `workload` = booked days of INVITED and ACCEPTED assignments in `[start − 90, end + 90]`, clipped to the window. It excludes this mission.

**Scarcity data in the seed (org A).** Robotics has 2 holders (cara, hana). Each other skill has 3 holders. A scarcity term changes the result only when the gap is equal. Example: an EVA ≥ 3 slot has dev (gap 0, no other skill) and eli (gap 0, Geology). Dev wins on scarcity before workload counts, even though dev has 12 booked days in December.

**Risk: workload only as a tie breaker.** The product promise is "makes sure that they are not overloaded" (`design/DESIGN.md:6`). Effect: an exact-fit member with high workload always beats a free member with gap 1. The options are below.

questions.question: In which order does the cost compare gap and scarcity? Workload is the last tie breaker in each option.

options.label: gap > scarcity > workload
options.description: Strict order. Scarcity splits only candidates with an equal gap. Workload splits only an equal gap and equal scarcity. Easy to explain in the P1 rank breakdown.

options.label: (gap + scarcity) > workload
options.description: One combined score, then workload. A gap-0 member who is the only holder of a rare skill (scarcity 1.0) ties with a gap-1 member with no other skills.

options.label: scarcity > gap > workload
options.description: Keep holders of rare skills free first, then use the closest fit.

questions.question: How do we compute the scarcity of a member for a slot? holders(skill) = the number of crew members in the org with that skill at any level. The slot skill is excluded.

options.label: Max of 1/holders
options.description: Only the rarest other skill counts. A member with many common skills is not penalized. Sole holder: 1.0. Example: Cara (Robotics, 2 holders) = 0.5.

options.label: Sum of 1/holders
options.description: Each other skill adds to the cost. Effect: a generalist with 5 common skills (5 x 0.33 = 1.67) ranks lower than a sole holder of one rare skill (1.0).

options.label: Count of rare skills
options.description: Count the other skills with 2 holders or fewer. An integer, easy to show. The threshold is a code constant.

options.label: Tie breaker only
options.description: As in your note. Workload never overrides gap or scarcity. P2 'Additional resource constraints' can add a cap later.

options.label: Tie breaker + hard cap

options.label: gap > scarcity > workload
options.description: Strict order. Scarcity splits only candidates with an equal gap. Workload splits only an equal gap and equal scarcity. Easy to explain in the P1 rank breakdown.

options.label: (gap + scarcity) > workload
options.description: One combined score, then workload. A gap-0 member who is the only holder of a rare skill (scarcity 1.0) ties with a gap-1 member with no other skills.

options.label: scarcity > gap > workload
options.description: Keep holders of rare skills free first, then use the closest fit.

questions.question: How do we compute the scarcity of a member for a slot? holders(skill) = the number of crew members in the org with that skill at any level. The slot skill is excluded.

options.label: Max of 1/holders
options.description: Only the rarest other skill counts. A member with many common skills is not penalized. Sole holder: 1.0. Example: Cara (Robotics, 2 holders) = 0.5.

options.label: Sum of 1/holders
options.description: Each other skill adds to the cost. Effect: a generalist with 5 common skills (5 x 0.33 = 1.67) ranks lower than a sole holder of one rare skill (1.0).

options.label: Count of rare skills
options.description: Count the other skills with 2 holders or fewer. An integer, easy to show. The threshold is a code constant.

questions.question: How does the matcher protect crew members from overload (DESIGN.md:6)?

options.label: Tie breaker only
options.description: As in your note. Workload never overrides gap or scarcity. P2 'Additional resource constraints' can add a cap later.

options.label: Tie breaker + hard cap
options.description: Also add a filter: exclude a member with more than N booked days in the window. N is a code constant (example: 60). This adds a new hard rule to DESIGN.md.

options.label: Workload in the score

        AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unavailability n WHERE n.user_id = c.user_id

        AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM assignment a JOIN mission m ON m.id = a.mission_id
            WHERE a.user_id = c.user_id AND {ACTIVE}
            AND m.start_date <= :e AND :s <= m.end_date)"""
    free = rows(conn, sql, s=start, e=end)

The design now has all inputs. Kai changes the seed to 20 users and 5 missions. The README lists the seed users and counts (`README.md:40-64`), so the plan updates it too.

**Approaches for the code structure**

1. **Pure solver module + loader (recommended).** A new `mc_api/matcher.py` holds a pure function with no DB access. Input: slots and candidates. Output: one suggestion or none per slot. The router loads the data through `OrgScope` and calls the function. Unit tests prove the cost rules without Postgres.
2. **All in the router.** This gives fewer files, but each ranking test then needs the DB.
3. **SQL eligibility + Python solver.** One SQL query computes eligibility and workload. This is fast for large orgs, but harder to read. P2 lists "Optimization for large orgs" (`design/DESIGN.md:104`).

**Design**

*A. API.* The new route is `GET /missions/{mission_id}/match`. It is read-only and writes no rows. The checks run in this order: 404 for another org or a missing ID, then 403 for a non-owner with the role and the rule, then 409 if the status is not DRAFT. A crew member gets 403 from the router guard. The response type in `mc_shared` is `MatchPreview`: `mission_id` and a list of `{slot: SlotOut, suggestion: CrewSuggestion | None}` in slot order. `CrewSuggestion` has `user_id`, `username`, `display_name`, `level` and `workload_days`. Archived slots are not in the list.

*B. Filters.* The matcher uses the five filters from my first message. The decliner filter applies in DRAFT too: a DECLINED row stays after a withdraw to DRAFT (`design/DESIGN.md:241`). The "open slots only" rule does not apply in DRAFT, because a DRAFT mission has no INVITED or ACCEPTED rows (`design/DESIGN.md:268`). Step 7 adds it.

*C. Solver.* `linear_sum_assignment` gets a slots × candidates matrix. `BIG` marks the ineligible pairs, so the solver fills the maximum number of slots first. The cost order is gap, then scarcity (max of `1/holders` over the other skills), then workload, then username A–Z. The plan encodes this order exactly, without float ties. `holders` counts the CREW members of the org with the skill at any level.

*D. Workload.* It is the sum of the days of each INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment, clipped to `[start − 90, end + 90]`, with both ends included. `WORKLOAD_WINDOW_DAYS = 90` is a code constant.

*E. CLI.* The command is `mc missions match <mission-id>`. It prints a table: Slot, Skill, Min level, Crew, Level, Workload days. An unfilled slot shows "No match". The last line is "N of M slots filled". The exit code is 0 when slots stay unfilled, and 1 on an API error.

*F. Seed and docs.* The seed adds `kai` (Kai Mensah, CREW, EVA 3) and a DRAFT mission "Polar Ice Survey": lead `leo`, 2027-01-11 to 2027-01-24, slots Piloting ≥ 3, EVA ≥ 3 and Medicine ≥ 2. The expected preview is ben, kai, gus. The plan also updates the README and replaces the "To evaluate" lines in `design/DESIGN.md:402,406`, with a "Changes" row. The API gets the new dependency `scipy`, which brings numpy.

*G. Tests.*
- Unit tests prove the solver: global against greedy, maximum fill, gap, scarcity, workload, the username tie and more slots than candidates.
- Integration tests prove each filter with the date boundaries, the workload clipping, archived slots and the RBAC errors (crew 403, other lead 403, other org 404, non-DRAFT 409).
- An E2E test runs `mc missions match` on the seeded mission as `leo`, and the error paths as `lena` and `nick`.

# Spec: missions-draft

## Goal
Add DRAFT missions: create, edit, slots, list and show, in the API and the CLI (build step 4, `design/DESIGN.md:67`). Add the skill list, so that a lead can find skill IDs for slots. Move the API routes into a `routers` package and the CLI commands into a `commands` package, so that each later build step adds one module.

## Acceptance criteria
| ID | Criterion | The tests must prove |
|---|---|---|
| AC1 | The API follows the FastAPI "Bigger Applications" structure. The CLI has one module for each command group. Behaviour does not change. | `mc_api/main.py` contains no route function. Each router is in `mc_api/routers/`. `get_current_user` and `get_scope` are in `mc_api/dependencies.py`. The CLI commands are in `mc_cli/commands/`. All Step 3 tests pass without a change of their assertions. |
| AC2 | A director or a lead creates a mission (DESIGN 327). | `POST /missions` gives 201. The status is `DRAFT`. `lead_id` is the caller. The response has no slots. |
| AC3 | The API flags a mission that a director leads (DESIGN 199, 339-341). | `requires_additional_director` is true when the current role of the lead is `DIRECTOR`. It is false for a lead. A role change of the lead in the DB changes the flag of the existing mission. |
| AC4 | The API rejects wrong dates. | `end_date < start_date` gives 422 on create. On edit, the API checks the dates after it merges them with the stored values. A wrong merge gives 422. |
| AC5 | Directors and leads list all missions of the own org (DESIGN 331). | `GET /missions` returns each mission of the own org and no mission of another org. The order is newest `start_date` first. |
| AC6 | Directors and leads show a mission of the own org. | `GET /missions/{id}` returns the mission, the lead username, the flag and the active slots in position order. Archived slots are not in the response. |
| AC7 | The lead of the mission edits title, description and dates in DRAFT (DESIGN 273). | `PATCH /missions/{id}` with some fields changes only those fields. It gives 200 and the new mission. |
| AC8 | Only the lead of the mission edits it (DESIGN 323). | Another lead or a director of the own org gets 403 on PATCH and on both slot routes. The body is `{"role": "<ROLE>", "rule": "Directors and leads edit only their own missions"}`. |
| AC9 | Edits are allowed only in DRAFT (DESIGN 273). | For a mission in each other status, PATCH and both slot routes give 409. The body is `{"detail": "Mission is <STATUS>. Edits are allowed only in DRAFT."}`. |
| AC10 | The lead adds a slot in DRAFT (DESIGN 280-281). | `POST /missions/{id}/slots {skill_id, min_level}` gives 201 and the mission. The new slot has the lowest free position among the active slots. `min_level` outside 1 to 5 gives 422. |
| AC11 | The lead removes a slot in DRAFT. The API archives it (DESIGN 214, 283). | `DELETE /missions/{id}/slots/{position}` gives 200 and the mission without the slot. The row still exists with `archived_at` set. A position with no active slot gives 404. After the lead removes slot 2 of 3, the next new slot gets position 2. |
| AC12 | A slot names only a skill of the own org (DESIGN 355). | A `skill_id` that does not exist, or that belongs to another org, gives 422 with the body `{"detail": "Unknown skill: <id>"}`. Both cases give the same body. |
| AC13 | Crew members have no access to missions in this step (DESIGN 331). | A crew member gets 403 on each mission route, for each ID. The body is `{"role": "CREW", "rule": "Only directors and leads manage and view missions"}`. |
| AC14 | A mission of another org is not visible (DESIGN req 4, 22). | A director and a lead of org A each get 404 for a mission of org B on GET, PATCH, POST slots and DELETE slots. Each body equals the body for a random UUID: `{"detail": "Not found"}`. The mission of org B does not change. |
| AC15 | Each user lists the skills of the own org. | `GET /skills` gives 200 for each role. It returns `id`, `name` and `description` of each skill of the own org, sorted by name. It returns no skill of another org. |
| AC16 | The CLI runs the mission commands (DESIGN 423-425). | `mc missions create`, `edit`, `list`, `show`, `mc missions slots add` and `remove`, and `mc skills list` each call the API and show the result. `create` of a director-led mission prints "This mission needs an additional director for approval." |
| AC17 | The CLI shows a clear error for 409 and 422. | For 409, the output contains the `detail`. For 422 with a text `detail`, the output contains the text. For 422 with a FastAPI validation list, the output contains `<field>: <message>` for each item. Each exits 1 with no traceback. |

## Non-goals
- Slot update. The lead removes a slot and adds a new one.
- Filters for `mc missions list`.
- Crew access to mission details. Steps 7 and 9 add it through assignments.
- A way to clear the description.
- A schema change or a migration. The `mission` and `mission_requirement` tables of step 2 have all the columns.
- Submit, approve and the other transitions (step 6 and step 8). The matcher (step 5).
- Short references for missions and skills (P1, DESIGN 82).
- An `internal/` package. Step 4 has no admin routes.

## End-to-end check
| # | Action | Expected result | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `mc login --user leo`, then `mc skills list` | Exit 0. The output has the 6 skills of "Artemis Space Agency" with their IDs. It does not have `Welding`. | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_missions_cli.py` |
| 2 | `mc missions create --title "Ice Core Drill" --start 2027-03-01 --end 2027-03-10` | Exit 0. The output has the mission ID and `DRAFT`. It has no additional director message. | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_missions_cli.py` |
| 3 | `mc missions slots add <id> --skill <Piloting id> --level 3`, then the same with `<Geology id> --level 2` | Exit 0 each. The output shows slot 1 Piloting and slot 2 Geology. | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_missions_cli.py` |
| 4 | `mc missions slots remove <id> 1`, then `mc missions slots add <id> --skill <EVA id> --level 3` | Exit 0 each. The output shows slot 1 EVA and slot 2 Geology. | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_missions_cli.py` |
| 5 | `mc missions edit <id> --title "Ice Core Drill II"` | Exit 0. The output has the new title. | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_missions_cli.py` |
| 6 | `mc missions list`, then `mc missions show <id>` | Exit 0 each. The list has the new mission and the 3 seeded missions of org A. `show` has the new title, `leo` and both slots. | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_missions_cli.py` |
| 7 | `mc login --user nick`, then `mc missions show <id>` | Exit 1. The output contains `Not found`. | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_missions_cli.py` |
| 8 | `mc login --user ava`, then `mc missions list` | Exit 1. The output contains `CREW` and `Only directors and leads manage and view missions`. | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_missions_cli.py` |
| 9 | `mc login --user diana`, then `mc missions create --title "Deep Field Survey" --start 2027-04-01 --end 2027-04-05` | Exit 0. The output contains `This mission needs an additional director for approval.` | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_missions_cli.py` |

The E2E test uses the seed data and uvicorn on a free port, as the Step 3 E2E test does (`packages/api/tests/e2e/test_auth_cli.py:21-47`).

## Resolved questions
| Question | Answer | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Task name? | `missions-draft`, folder `.work/missions-draft/` | me |
| Which state does Step 4 start from? | Step 3 is complete as `.work/auth-tenant/plan.md` describes it. This includes `OrgScope.get` and `select`, `Forbidden` with its 403 handler, and `GET /users/{id}`. | me, `.work/auth-tenant/plan.md:211-226` |
| How does the lead change slots? | Add and remove only. To change a slot, the lead removes it and adds a new one. The archived row keeps the assignment history. | me |
| Which position does a new slot get? | The lowest free position among the active slots | me |
| How does the CLI name a skill? | By UUID, as DESIGN says for P0. `GET /skills` and `mc skills list` show the IDs. | me, `design/DESIGN.md:437` |
| Who can list skills? | Each role, own org only | me |

## Acceptance criteria

| AC1 | The lead of a DRAFT mission runs the matcher preview (DESIGN 17, 329). The preview writes no rows. | `GET /missions/{id}/match` by the mission lead gives 200 and a `MatchPreview`. This is true for a lead and for a director who leads the mission. The row counts of all tables do not change. |
| AC2 | Only the lead of the mission runs the matcher in this step (DESIGN 324). | Another lead and a director of the own org each get 403. The body is `{"role": "<ROLE>", "rule": "Directors and leads run the matcher only on their own missions"}`. |

An ACCEPTED assignment on a mission that ends on 2027-02-28 → suggested. |

A crew member fills a maximum of one slot (DESIGN 282). | Unit, greedy trap: slot 1 EVA ≥ 3, slot 2 Robotics ≥ 3. Cara has EVA 4 and Robotics 3, dev has EVA 3, nobody else has Robotics. Result: slot 1 dev, slot 2 cara. Unit: 3 slots and 2 candidates who qualify for all 3 → 2 slots filled with 2 different members, 1 slot `null`. No member is in two slots of one preview. |

Gap wins over scarcity and workload: ben with a rare other skill and 60 workload days still beats ivan with gap 1 and no other skill and 0 days. |

Scarcity is the max of `1 / holders(skill)` over the other skills of the candidate, without the slot skill. `holders(skill)` is the number of CREW members of the org with that skill at any level. A candidate with no other skill has scarcity 0 (DESIGN 402). | Unit: slot EVA ≥ 3. dev (no other skill) and eli (Geology, 3 holders) both have gap 0 → dev. eli (Geology, 3 holders) against cara (Robotics, 2 holders), both gap 0 → eli.
